title: LiC11: Workforce Strategy: Designing a Workforce That Can Run, Serve, and Change
author: Richard Claydon
summary: Richard Claydon argues that most organisations facing a headcount-reduction debate do not have a headcount problem but a work-portfolio problem. Through a vignette of an executive team fighting over a ten percent cut, he splits work into three logics, Run, Serve and Change, and shows that Run always wins because it is measurable and punishable while Serve and Change are squeezed into the same exhausted people. He proposes treating the workforce as infrastructure and designing a portfolio of four segments, core strategic, stable operational, flexible or ecosystem, and sunset or legacy, each with different promises and risks. It is a Leadership piece because it concerns organisational design, management practice and how executives decide about people.
points: Headcount debates mislabel a problem of work design: nobody asks what work the workforce is being asked to do.
Run, Serve and Change are three distinct logics that are routinely packed into single jobs, and Run wins because it is visible and punished when it fails.
Serve work becomes invisible emotional labour and Change becomes side-of-desk theatre, eroding trust and stalling transformation.
Segmenting the workforce into core strategic, stable operational, flexible and sunset groups lets leaders make different promises to each.
Overloading context-holders with Run turns them into firefighters, while isolating them in Change detaches transformation from reality.
quotes: They didn’t have a headcount problem. They had a work portfolio problem they were trying to solve with a spreadsheet.
You forecast demand, calculate workloads, set productivity assumptions, and work backwards to an FTE number. You then argue about whether that number is affordable.
In most organisations, we don’t name these three. We wrap them together in a single job and hope people can juggle:
When you overload them with Run (“just help clear the backlog”) and transactional Serve (“jump on this escalation”), Change quietly dies. They become glorified firefighters.
Handled well, this segment is your navigational infrastructure. Handled badly, it is your most exhausted and cynical group.
Done right, this is the backbone you can build on. Done wrong, it’s the source of a slow, grinding legitimacy crisis.
